channel.title: The Dig — Calibration, tuning and drift
channel.description: Papers relevant to operating, benchmarking, integrating and using a semiconductor spin-qubit quantum computer of at least 16 qubits that is co-located with and integrated into an HPC system. Today's arXiv announcement, ranked against the Calibration, tuning and drift preset. Today’s ranked reading list centers on silicon spin-qubit hardware and operational benchmarking: 2611.12850 proposes over-gate TiN stressors to enhance valley splitting in Si/SiGe wiggle-well dots, 2611.14114 offers a cloud-executed GHZ-fidelity benchmark that tests whether calibration data predict processor performance, and 2611.12217 maps how multi-dot configurations affect electron temperature and double-dot latching for initialization and readout. The skim-tier items broaden the context but sit further from current spin-qubit operation: 2611.13301 presents an MLIR-based fault-tolerant compiler, 2611.12779 a neutral-atom arbitrary two-qubit gate architecture, 2611.13371 silicon-spin qLDPC syndrome extraction with mobile ancillas, 2611.14422 a QRAM energetic-cost accounting method, and 2611.13796 an analog Rydberg-atom QAOA MaxCut study. No pay dirt today — 2 to read.

item.title: Enhancing valley splitting in Si/SiGe Wiggle Well quantum dots through integrated stressor-gate architectures
item.description:
Read new result — Compressively stressed surface TiN thin films induce shear strains exceeding 0.1% in underlying Si/SiGe quantum wells even when routed across gate stacks, yielding deterministic valley splittings above 100 μeV in long-period Wiggle Wells.

Grade 0.405 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Colloquium : Advances in automation of quantum dot devices control”

Figure

Linecuts of shear strain across dot and charge-sensor channels in a realistic quad-dot device layout, showing induced εxy sustained above 0.1% across multiple dots.

Asks

Can surface-deposited thin-film stressors generate and maintain the shear strain required for deterministic valley splitting in Si/SiGe Wiggle Well quantum dots when integrated with realistic gate stacks?

Before

Conventional gate electrodes generate shear strains of ~0.01% to ~0.025%, 4-10 times too small for strain-assisted Wiggle Wells.

But

Numerical continuum elastic simulation rather than experimental fabrication; assumes residual stress is thickness-independent; high-strain region is narrow, limiting scalability beyond 1D to narrow multi-row quantum dot arrays.

Tools

finite-element modeling (COMSOL Multiphysics) · TiN thin-film stressors · Si/SiGe Wiggle Well heterostructures

Abstract

Engineering large and reproducible valley splittings is essential for the scalable operation of silicon spin qubits. In Si/SiGe quantum dot devices, valley splitting arises predominantly from atomic-scale disorder and is therefore inherently random, motivating approaches that introduce a large deterministic contribution. Strain-assisted Wiggle Wells provide a route to deterministic valley splitting by combining an oscillatory Ge concentration in the Si well with shear strain; however, generating the required strain in a manner compatible with large-scale architectures remains a challenge. Here, we propose patterned stressed thin films as a scalable approach for generating shear strain in the quantum well of Si/SiGe quantum dot devices. Finite-element simulations show that compressively stressed TiN films can generate shear strains exceeding 0.1% at the quantum well, sufficient for deterministic valley splittings of hundreds of μeV in strain-assisted Wiggle Wells. We show that this strain can extend across multiple quantum dots and is maintained in realistic gate geometries, providing a fabrication-compatible approach for scaling deterministic valley splitting to quantum dot arrays.

item.title: Impact of multi-dot configurations on electron temperature and double quantum dot latching in gate-controlled qubit devices
item.description:
Read new result — Using a biased single-electron transistor concurrently as charge sensor and reservoir heats the reservoir electron temperature to 229 mK at 50 µV bias and 799 mK at 250 µV, compared to 133 mK and 152 mK for an unbiased extended reservoir.

Grade 0.488 · 3.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Colloquium : Advances in automation of quantum dot devices control”

Figure

Fermi fit broadening of the 0-1 transition plotted against mixing plate temperature for 50 µV, 150 µV, and 250 µV SET bias. It compares loading from an extended reservoir with loading from a dual-role reservoir-sensor SET, showing higher electron temperatures in the latter.

Asks

How does using a single-electron transistor simultaneously as a charge sensor and electron reservoir impact the probed electron temperature, spectroscopy, and double quantum dot latching behavior in spin qubit architectures?

Before

Extended reservoir baseline was 133 mK at 50 µV SET bias and 152 mK at 250 µV SET bias in the same device.

But

Measured on two devices; dilution refrigerator base temperature < 10 mK; latching observability depends on integration time per point being shorter than the direct tunneling time (20 ms).

Tools

Si/SiGe heterostructure quantum dots · Single-electron transistor (SET) charge sensing · Pulsed gate spectroscopy (PGS) · Dilution refrigerator base temperature below 10 mK

Abstract

Many currently envisaged scalable architectures for Si/SiGe spin qubit devices utilize gate-controlled multi-dot configurations characterized by their peculiar Coulomb blockade physics. One example is the concurrent use of a single electron transistor (SET) as a charge sensor and as a reservoir for adjacent qubit quantum dots (QD). We find that the SET energy spectrum impacts pulsed gate spectroscopy of the QD when the SET simultaneously acts as the reservoir and the sensor. Then, using the qubit QD as a probe, we quantify how strongly the electron temperature of the SET depends on the applied bias. It surpasses a reference experiment by 100 mK even at 50 μV bias. Our results provide a strong incentive for choosing spin qubit initialization schemes which do not rely on coupling to the reservoir in such devices. Switching to a double quantum dot connected to a single reservoir, a frequent configuration for qubit readout, we finally demonstrate the tunability of the characteristic latching behavior by systematically mapping it in the few-electron stability diagram.

item.arxave:action: Include characterization of reservoir-sensor SET bias versus qubit-QD electron temperature in the device tuning and calibration checklist, and record the chosen bias in calibration metadata.
The paper shows biased SET reservoirs broaden electron temperature and can degrade reservoir-based spin initialization; readout schemes should be assessed for whether they rely on reservoir loading.

arxave:action.title: Optimal SET bias for sensing vs temperature

item.arxave:action: What SET bias range preserves adequate charge-sensing signal-to-noise while keeping the adjacent qubit QD electron temperature low enough for the intended initialization and readout fidelity?
